title: Distributed and Mixed-Precision Training
overview: Large models need many GPUs and efficient numerics. Data and model parallelism split the work, while mixed precision uses 16-bit math to save memory and time.
objectives: Compare data, tensor and pipeline parallelism
Explain loss scaling in fp16 training
Use gradient accumulation to emulate large batches

method.title: Data parallelism
method.body: Each device holds a model copy and processes a shard of the batch; gradients are averaged with all-reduce.

method.title: Model parallelism
method.body: Layers (pipeline) or individual matrices (tensor) are split across devices when the model does not fit on one.

method.title: Mixed precision
method.body: Compute in fp16 or bf16 while keeping fp32 master weights; fp16 needs loss scaling to avoid gradient underflow, bf16 usually does not.

method.title: Accumulation
method.body: Summing gradients over several micro-batches before stepping simulates a larger batch on limited memory.

playground.starterCode:
import numpy as np
g = np.float32(1e-9)
print("fp32 gradient:", g)
print("fp16 gradient:", np.float16(g))           # underflows to 0
scale = np.float32(2 ** 16)
g16 = np.float16(g * scale)
print("scaled fp16:", g16, "-> unscaled:", np.float32(g16) / scale)
shards = [np.array([1.0, 2.0]), np.array([3.0, 4.0])]
print("all-reduce mean:", np.mean(shards, axis=0))
